newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine unions block roads, close businesses.
newsitem.headline: Argentine unions block roads, close businesses.

text.p: Unions manned roadblocks throughout Argentina and closed many provincial firms on Thursday, but support was lukewarm in Buenos Aires for a general strike boycotted by workers loyal to the government.
"The government cannot deny...that there is a strike throughout the country," Victor de Gennaro, leader of the CTA public sector workers union, told local television.
The CTA and MTA opposition unions called the 24-hour strike to protest against 16.1 percent unemployment and proposed labor market reforms.
But the country's main union federation, the CGT, which had reached a deal with the government on labor reforms, opposed the strike.
The political opposition, reluctant to alarm voters before October congressional elections, said strikers were right to be angry but wrong to stop work.
The grain port of Necochea was closed and protesters cut roads to the cities of Rosario and Cordoba, where many businesses closed and public transport was off the streets, media reported.
Roadblocks isolated the capital of the poor northwestern province of Jujuy, San Salvador, and in the south cut the road between the Patagonian provinces of Neuquen and Rio Negro.
In Buenos Aires, state schools gave pupils a holiday and the government said buses were operating only at a fifth of the normal level.

But other transport, including flights from Ezeiza international airport, was almost normal. With bus services at a trickle, traffic clogged roads into the city center and, once they reached downtown, people went to work -- or to the cafes -- as usual.

A small group of demonstrators burnt tires at a roadblock in the center of Buenos Aires' seedy entertaintment district, and some other roadblocks sprung up around the city. In some areas, gangs of masked youths brandished sticks and stones.

No significant violence had been reported by midday (1500 GMT). Striking unions planned no major march or demonstration, but the government deployed extra police and said they would suppress any disturbances.
Presidential Chief of Staff Alberto Kohan told local radio that the strike was "without any sort of objective" and problems should be settled through the democratic process.

The CGT, with strong links to President Carlos Menem's Peronist Party, has written the strike off as "the weakest and most confused in the history of unionism." Opposition unions claim the CGT has sold out the workers.
The general strike was Argentina's fourth in just over a year. The previous strikes were organized by the CGT.
